data.answer:
Year-to-year swings in plant breeder’s rights (PBR) numbers can reflect small filing volumes and administrative timing, rather than changes in underlying breeding investment.[1][2]

- **Small numbers amplify fluctuations.** PBR volumes are modest, so relatively small changes can produce large percentage movements. Filing totals are also strongly influenced by a small number of large breeding programs.[1]
- **Applications and registrations operate on different timelines.** Registration typically takes around 2.5 years, including substantive examination and a comparative growing trial, so registrations in one year need not reflect applications made that year.[3]
- **Processing conditions can shift registrations between years.** The 2024 report suggests the 2023 registration increase may partly reflect resumed field examinations after COVID-19 restrictions and changes encouraging overdue applications to progress.[4]

For example, the 2026 report records applications falling 6.4% to 264 in 2025 while registrations rose from 124 to 169. It attributes the registration rebound to examination timing and pipeline dynamics—not a structural shift in filing behaviour.[2]

citations.quote: Compared with patents and trade marks, total PBR volumes are modest. As a result, annual movements can appear pronounced even when underlying breeding investment remains steady. Interpretation therefore requires caution: year-to-year volatility often reflects the behaviour of a small number of large breeding programs.

claims.text: Small PBR volumes amplify percentage movements, and a small number of large breeding programs can strongly influence annual totals even when underlying breeding investment remains steady.

citations.quote: In 2025, PBR applications fell by 6.4%, from 282 in 2024 to 264 (Figure 5.1). This marks the third consecutive annual decline.
Registrations increased from 124 in 2024 to 169 in 2025. The rise reflects examination timing and pipeline dynamics rather than a structural shift in filing behaviour.

claims.text: In 2025, applications fell 6.4% to 264 while registrations increased from 124 to 169; the 2026 report attributes the registration rise to examination timing and pipeline dynamics rather than a structural shift in filing behaviour.

citations.quote: Though timeframes vary by plant type, the process of registering a PBR typically takes around 2.5 years. This is because the application must pass a substantive examination process and a comparative growing trial.
There is little correlation between filings in a year and registrations in the same year, since most applications take more than 12 months to register.

claims.text: Registration typically takes around 2.5 years and requires substantive examination and a comparative growing trial, so same-year applications and registrations need not correspond.

citations.quote: The significant rise in registrations Year in 2023 may reflect the resumption of field examinations after the COVID-19 pandemic, when travel restrictions made growing trials harder to organise and attend.

In 2023 IP Australia introduced changes that have moved customers to progress their applications toward an outcome (e.g., grant or withdrawal) where the applicant was overdue in providing a detailed description of their plant variety. The change has likely contributed to the increase in registrations.

claims.text: The 2024 report suggests resumed field examinations after COVID-19 restrictions and changes progressing overdue applications may have contributed to increased registrations in 2023.
